text:
viv: heads-up: hit a tricky UX while integrating generator streaming into our reverse-proxy. auth refresh + client disconnect interaction is messy and leads to leaked goroutines. opening thread to discuss API surface we should expose.

viv: simplified handler that reproduces the leak:

```go
func streamProxy(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
  ctx := r.Context()
  it := sdk.Generator("alpha").Stream(ctx, prompt)
  defer it.Close()
  for it.Next() {
    if ctx.Err() != nil {
      return
    }
    _, _ = w.Write([]byte(it.Value()))
    w.(http.Flusher).Flush()
  }
}
```

viv: problem: when auth refresh blocks, Next() is stuck in handshake/retry and closing the connection doesn't unblock the handler immediately. Close() is only effective after the handshake path finishes.

sam: ouch. We should consider *two* API axes: per-call cancellation (Next(ctx)) vs. explicit interrupt (Stream.CloseNow()/Cancel()). different ergonomics for different call sites.

noah: another option: provide a reader-like adaptor: StreamAsReader(ctx) io.ReadCloser that yields bytes and respects ctx cancellation on Read(). handlers can then use io.Copy with request ctx-aware readers.

rachael: Reader-adaptor is neat for generic handlers, but it hides message boundaries (if generator returns discrete tokens). Not ideal for token-by-token flush.

viv: agreed. we want token flush for latency-sensitive UIs. Reader loses granularity unless we encode separators. Also tests show it doesn't map well to token-level metrics.

sam: what about a channel-based API: func (s *Stream) Deliver(ctx, ch chan<- string) error — the SDK pushes parts into channel and reacts to ctx cancel by closing channel and returning. That aligns with Go concurrency primitives.

noah: channel API looks ergonomic for apps that want backpressure: if the channel is unbuffered, the SDK naturally blocks on send until consumer reads. But it's a breaking change for some callers and leaks if users don't drain the channel.

rachael: for HTTP handlers the simplest is Next(ctx) because it composes with r.Context() and doesn't require remembering to Close in early returns. We should make the internal handshake/token refresh take a ctx too so it returns early with context.Canceled.

viv: implementation must also ensure that when Next(ctx) returns false and Err() is context.Canceled, we don't attempt automatic reconnects. Caller intent should be respected.

sam: also think about distinguishing errors: ErrCanceled vs ErrClientGone vs auth errors. We could reuse context.Canceled and also export ErrClientDisconnected. But minimal surface: document that context.Canceled is raised when caller cancels.

noah: test plan idea: create httptest.Server + fake auth server that sleeps on refresh. Make client close connection mid-refresh and assert the server handler goroutine exits within 200ms. Add a helper in testutil to detect goroutine leaks by counting live goroutines before/after.

rachael: for backwards compatibility: keep Stream(ctx) but mark as "not guaranteed to be cancellable during auth refresh" and recommend Next(ctx) for handlers. Provide a migration snippet in README.

viv: +1. Also we should add a sample app (proxy sample) to devex examples showing both patterns (Next(ctx) and channel) and demonstrate test that fails on current master. That helps reviewers run locally.

sam: small API nit: Next(ctx) vs NextWith(ctx) — prefer plain Next(ctx). And Err() should reflect last failure. If handshake canceled return context.Canceled from Err().

noah: one more edge: what if auth refresh succeeds very quickly but the user canceled just before it finished? we need to ensure the SDK checks ctx right after handshake completes and aborts before reading more stream frames. otherwise we might deliver a stray token after caller gave up.

rachael: good catch. handshake code should check ctx on both entry and exit points. Add a tiny retry/backoff jitter but always honoring ctx between attempts.

ci-bot: Created draft PR #4512: "go/sdk: iterator.Next(ctx) + cancellable auth refresh; add proxy sample & leak test" — reviewers: @sam @rachael @noah

viv: thanks — i'll attach the proxy sample, the failing test harness, and a brief README section showing migration. If folks prefer we can also prototype the channel and reader adapters later, but Next(ctx) is the lowest-friction for HTTP handlers.

sam: LGTM. please include a benchmark measuring token latency before/after to ensure we don't add significant overhead to the hot path.

noah: will do. Also add a small note about how this interacts with our retry policy: "if canceled by caller, do not retry".

viv: perfect. i'll push a proper PR and assign reviewers.
